The Chemistry Behind Liquid Products

Before you formulate a full range, you need three tools of thought: which surfactant family does which job, how pH changes safety and performance, and how to keep a water-based product free of germs for its whole shelf life. This module gives you those tools, with the arithmetic you will use in every later lesson.
Surfactant families and how to calculate active matter
Name the four surfactant families and give one raw material from each

Every product in this course, from hand wash to fabric softener, is built on **surfactants**. The word is short for surface active agent. A surfactant molecule has two ends: a **head that loves water** and a **tail that loves oil**. That double nature is what lets water, which normally runs off grease, grab the grease and carry it away.
A woman working with laboratory flasks
Formulating is applied chemistry: you choose each raw material for the job its molecules do.
How a surfactant cleans

When you add enough surfactant to water, the tails hide from the water by gathering into tiny balls called **micelles**, with the heads facing outwards. Oil and greasy dirt slip inside the oily centre of the micelle. The micelle stays suspended in the water, so when you rinse, the dirt goes with it. The surfactant also lowers the surface tension of water, which is why soapy water wets a greasy plate instead of beading on it.

Water wets the surface
Tails grab the oil

Rinse water carries micelles

The same four molecular steps happen in a hand wash, a shampoo and a dish liquid.

Below a certain concentration, surfactant molecules float about singly and micelles do not form. Above it, extra surfactant goes into micelles that are ready to hold dirt. In practice this means a product needs a **minimum amount of real surfactant** to work, and that adding far more than needed mostly adds cost, not cleaning. Your test batches in later lessons will help you find the sensible middle for each product, using real dirty plates and real hands rather than guesswork.

The compatibility rule

Anionic and cationic surfactants attract each other and can form a sticky solid that does neither job. That is why a quaternary ammonium disinfectant (cationic) is weakened by soap or SLES left on a surface, and why fabric softener goes in the rinse, not with the detergent. Shampoo makers only combine them in small, controlled amounts, as you will see in Module 3.
Active matter: the number that matters

Surfactants are rarely sold pure. SLES paste is commonly about **70% active**, meaning 100 g of paste holds about 70 g of real surfactant and 30 g of water. CAPB is usually a liquid around **30% active**. Always read the figure on your supplier's certificate or data sheet, because it changes between suppliers. The **active matter** of your finished product is the total weight of real surfactant in it, written as a percentage. It is the best single number for comparing strength and cost, and it is how you keep every batch the same when you change supplier.
Worked example: active matter of a 5 kg test formula
For example, Bisi in Ibadan writes a test formula for a mild hand wash: 15% SLES (70% active) and 6% CAPB (30% active), the rest water and additives. She wants to know the real surfactant content.
SLES contribution: 15% x 0.70 = 10.5% active.
CAPB contribution: 6% x 0.30 = 1.8% active.
Total active matter: 10.5% + 1.8% = 12.3%.
In a 5 kg batch: 5,000 g x 12.3 / 100 = 615 g of real surfactant.
Her new supplier's SLES is only 60% active. To keep 10.5% active from SLES she needs 10.5 / 0.60 = 17.5% of the new paste, so 875 g instead of 750 g in 5 kg.
Bisi records 12.3% active matter on her formula sheet. When raw material strength changes, she recalculates the paste weight so the finished product stays the same strength.

Measuring and adjusting pH for safe, stable products

**pH** tells you how acidic or alkaline a water-based liquid is, on a scale from 0 to 14. Pure water is 7, which is neutral. Below 7 is acidic (lime juice, vinegar). Above 7 is alkaline (caustic soda solution, bleach). The scale is **logarithmic**: pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5 and a hundred times more acidic than pH 6. A small number change is a big chemical change.
A test tube holding a liquid sample

Why pH matters in your range

**Skin and hair comfort.** The surface of healthy skin is slightly acidic, and products far from neutral can leave hands dry or irritated. Hair cuticles lie flatter at a slightly acidic pH, which is why shampoos and conditioners are usually made mildly acidic.
**Preservative performance.** Some preservatives, such as sodium benzoate, only work well in acidic products. The wrong pH can leave a product unprotected.
**Thickness.** SLES and CAPB blends thicken differently at different pH values, so a pH change can make a batch thinner or thicker.
**Cleaning power.** Acid dissolves limescale and rust stains; alkali cuts fats and oils. Hard-surface cleaners use this deliberately.
**Stability of actives.** Fabric softener esterquats break down when the pH is too high; bleach loses strength faster when it is not kept alkaline.

Measuring pH properly

**Universal indicator strips** are cheap and good enough to tell pH 5 from pH 8. Dip, wait the time on the pack, and compare the colour in daylight. Coloured products can confuse the reading, so test before adding dye. A **pen-type digital pH meter** is more precise. It must be **calibrated** with buffer solutions, usually pH 7 and pH 4, before a session, and rinsed with clean water between samples. A meter that is never calibrated gives confident wrong numbers. Thick products can coat the sensor; many makers test a 10% dilution in distilled water and note on their record that the reading was diluted, so every batch is tested the same way.

Adjusting a sample first stops you from overshooting a whole batch.
Worked example: lowering the pH of a 20 kg shampoo batch

For example, Amaka in Onitsha finishes a 20 kg shampoo batch and her calibrated meter reads pH 7.4. She wants about pH 6. She uses a 20% citric acid solution (20 g citric acid dissolved in 80 g water).
She weighs 200 g of shampoo into a clean cup. That is 1% of the batch (200 / 20,000 = 0.01).
She adds 0.5 g of citric solution, stirs and tests: pH 6.6. She adds another 0.4 g: pH 6.0.
Total used on the sample: 0.9 g. Scale up: 0.9 g x 100 = 90 g of solution for 20 kg.
That 90 g contains 90 x 0.20 = 18 g of citric acid.
To avoid overshooting, she adds about 80% first (72 g), stirs well, tests, then adds the rest in small portions until the meter shows about 6.
The batch reaches pH 6.0 without overshooting. Amaka writes "90 g of 20% citric solution per 20 kg" on the batch record, so the next batch starts with a known figure.
Handling acids and alkalis

Wear gloves and goggles when making adjuster solutions. Always add acid or caustic slowly **to water**, never water to a pile of concentrated chemical, because heat and splashing can result. Label every adjuster bottle clearly with its name and strength, and keep it away from food containers and children.

To raise a pH that is too low, use a dilute alkali such as a 10% sodium hydroxide solution or a little triethanolamine, in the same sample-first way. Raising pH needs more care than lowering it, because caustic is corrosive and a tiny excess can push a hand wash well past 8.

Finally, measure pH at the same stage every time, ideally after all ingredients are in and the batch has cooled and rested for a few hours. Fragrance, preservative and some thickeners nudge the pH, and a warm batch can read differently from a cool one. Write the reading, the meter used and whether it was a neat or diluted sample on your batch record. Over a few batches you will see a pattern, and you will know your normal starting pH before you even test.

Liquid soap and shampoo are mostly water, and water with a little sugar, protein or plant extract is food for bacteria and mould. A contaminated bottle may smell sour, grow black spots, separate, lose its thickness or swell as gas builds up. Worse, a product meant to clean can spread germs. **Preservation has two parts: keep germs out during production, and add a preservative that stops the few that get in later**, for example when a customer opens the bottle with wet hands.

Always ask your supplier for the **recommended use level** and **pH range** of the exact grade you buy, and write it on your formula sheet. More preservative is not better: too much can irritate skin, and too little lets germs win. Add most preservatives **near the end**, when the batch is below about 40 degrees Celsius, because heat can damage some of them.

For example, Hauwa in Kaduna is making 25 kg of hand wash at pH 6.2. Her supplier's phenoxyethanol blend data sheet gives a use level of 0.5% to 1.0%, and pH 3 to 12. She chooses 0.8%.
She confirms her pH (6.2) is inside the supplier's range, so this preservative suits the product.
Preservative weight: 25,000 g x 0.8 / 100 = 200 g.
She weighs 200 g on a digital scale, not with a cup, because small errors matter at this level.
She adds it after the batch has cooled, stirs for 5 minutes, then records "0.8%, 200 g, supplier lot number" on her batch sheet.
The batch is protected at a level inside the supplier's guidance, and anyone reading the batch record can see exactly what went in.
Keeping germs out in the first place
Clean production checklist
Treated or boiled, cooled water
Washed, sanitised drums and paddles
Clean hands, gloves, hair covered
New or sanitised bottles
Fill, cap and label quickly
A preservative cannot rescue a batch made with dirty water or equipment.
**Water:** borehole and tank water can carry many bacteria. Use treated water, or boil water and let it cool covered. Keep the water drum covered.
**Equipment:** wash with detergent, rinse, then wipe or rinse with 70% alcohol and let it dry. Use equipment only for production, never for food.
**Containers:** buy new bottles or wash and sanitise returned ones. Do not refill a customer's bottle you have not cleaned.
**Workspace:** a covered, swept room away from cooking, animals and dust. Keep raw materials off the floor on pallets.

Natural extracts such as aloe vera gel, hibiscus or rice water make a label attractive, but they also carry sugars and plant material that feed microbes. If you add them, use small amounts, buy preserved commercial extracts where possible, and watch your retained samples closely. A plain, well-preserved product is safer than a rich-sounding one that spoils on the shelf.
A simple shelf-life check

Large companies run formal stability and challenge tests in laboratories. A small producer can still learn a lot with **retained samples**. From every batch, keep two filled bottles. Put one on a shelf at room temperature and one in the warmest place you safely have, such as a closed storeroom under a roof. Check them every week for four weeks, then monthly, and record smell, colour, clarity, thickness, pH and any swelling. Also open and close the room-temperature bottle each week with clean hands, as a customer would, because real use introduces germs that a sealed bottle never meets. Keep the records with the batch sheet so you can answer any customer complaint with facts. If the warm sample changes within a month, do not promise a long shelf life. Before claiming a shelf life on a NAFDAC-registered product, follow the guidance NAFDAC gives you for your product category.
Your own safety when handling raw materials

Read the Safety Data Sheet for every chemical before first use. Wear nitrile gloves and goggles when handling concentrates, preservatives and fragrance oils, and a dust mask for powders such as SLS. Work with good ventilation, keep an eyewash bottle of clean water nearby, and store chemicals in their original labelled containers, out of reach of children.

The plate-washing test

Hands, pH and honest labels

Aim for a pH around neutral, about 6 to 8, so hands that soak for long periods are not irritated. Test pH with the method from Module 1. Avoid adding caustic soda or soda ash "for extra power" to a finished dish liquid: it raises pH, irritates skin and can dull aluminium pots. If you use sulphonic acid, make sure it is fully neutralised before the product leaves your hands.
Keep it out of drink bottles

Never pack dish liquid in used soft-drink or water bottles. A child or adult may drink from it by mistake. Use proper detergent bottles with your label, the words "Keep out of reach of children" and first aid instructions such as "If swallowed, rinse mouth and seek medical advice."

Restaurants and canteens often buy 4-litre or 20-litre kegs. For these buyers, your plate test result is a selling tool: "5 ml washes about 18 plates in our test" is a specific, checkable statement. Do not turn it into a claim you cannot support, such as "kills germs" or "twice as strong as any brand".

Repeat the plate test whenever you change a raw material supplier or your SLES level. A new drum that is a few percent weaker in active matter can quietly cut your plates per dose, and a restaurant customer will notice before you do. Keeping the test results in the same notebook as your batch records lets you spot that drift early.

Customers equate thickness with quality, even though thickness does not clean. A thin, watery hand wash looks cheap; one that will not pour looks spoiled. In this lesson you learn to **measure** thickness so every batch matches, to add colour precisely, and to fix the faults that make producers lose customers.

Measuring thickness with a flow test

Laboratories measure viscosity with a viscometer. You can get repeatable results with a **flow-time test**: take a 60 ml plastic syringe with the plunger removed, block the tip with your finger, fill it to the 50 ml mark with product at room temperature, release, and time with your phone how long it takes to drain to the 10 ml mark. Always use the same syringe, the same marks and a similar room temperature. Write the result in seconds. Your specification might say "flow time 15 to 25 seconds".
Finding the salt peak

In SLES and CAPB products, salt makes the micelles grow into long, tangled shapes, and the liquid thickens. But there is a **peak**: past a certain amount, adding more salt makes the product **thinner** again, and you cannot easily take salt out. So always test salt on small samples first.
Worked example: a salt step test for 20 kg of hand wash
For example, Ruth in Jos has a 20 kg batch of hand wash with pH already adjusted. Before adding salt to the drum, she takes four 200 g samples.
She adds salt to the samples at 0.5%, 1.0%, 1.5% and 2.0%: that is 1 g, 2 g, 3 g and 4 g in 200 g.
After stirring and resting 30 minutes, the flow times are 4, 9, 21 and 14 seconds.
Thickness rose up to 1.5% and fell at 2.0%, so the peak is around 1.5%. Her specification wants 15 to 25 seconds, so 1.5% fits.
For 20 kg: 20,000 g x 1.5 / 100 = 300 g of salt.
She dissolves the 300 g in 1,200 g of the batch's kept-back water to make a 20% brine (1,500 g), and adds it in three portions, testing after each.
The batch reaches about 20 seconds flow time without overshooting the peak. Ruth records "1.5% salt as 20% brine" so the next batch starts with a proven figure.

If a product is still too thin at its salt peak, you have other options: a little more CAPB, or a cellulose thickener such as hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC, often sold as nitrosol), dispersed slowly into the water at the start. Do not keep adding salt hoping for a different result.
Colour by numbers

Use **water-soluble cosmetic-grade dyes** for hand wash and shampoo. They are very strong, so weighing them directly is hard. Make a **1% stock solution**: dissolve 1 g of dye in 99 g of water, label it, and dose the stock. For example, if your target is 0.002% dye in a 20 kg batch, you need 20,000 x 0.002 / 100 = 0.4 g of dye, which is 40 g of the 1% stock, easy to weigh. Many dyes fade in sunlight, so store finished stock in shade and consider opaque bottles for light-sensitive colours.

Eyes and claims

Keep a simple feedback sheet for each tester and summarise the averages. If the next-day score is low, try raising CAPB by 1% and lowering SLES by 1% in a new test batch, keeping everything else the same. If lather is weak, check that your SLES is the strength you think it is before adding more. Busy customers, barbers and hotel housekeepers like a shampoo that leaves hair easy to comb without a separate conditioner. A **conditioning shampoo** does this with a small amount of a **cationic polymer**. In the bottle, the polymer stays dissolved with the surfactants. When you add water during rinsing, the mixture dilutes and some of the polymer, with surfactant, comes out of solution as a thin film that sticks to hair. Formulators call this film a **coacervate**. It smooths the hair surface, so it tangles less and feels softer.

Typical use levels for cationic polymers in shampoo are small, often a few tenths of a percent. Start with your supplier's recommendation. Too little gives no noticeable effect; too much can make hair feel heavy and coated over many washes, which customers call build-up.
Dispersing the powder without lumps

These powders swell on the outside the moment they touch water. If you tip them in all at once, you get lumps with dry powder inside, sometimes called fish eyes, that never dissolve. Two methods prevent this. First, **sprinkle slowly** onto fast-stirring water, before any surfactant goes in. Second, **make a slurry**: mix the powder into glycerin, which does not swell it, until smooth, then pour the slurry into the water while stirring.

She stirs for 30 minutes until the water is smooth and slightly thick, with no lumps, then continues the base method: EDTA, SLES, CAPB, panthenol and so on.

Buy two identical bundles of human hair from the market, or ask a volunteer with a full head of hair to allow a half-head test.
Wash one bundle (or half the head) with the standard shampoo and the other with the 2-in-1, using the same amount and rinse time.
While wet, comb each with the same wide-tooth comb. Count the strokes until the comb runs through freely, and note snagging.
Repeat on three separate days and average the results.

For example, if the standard shampoo needs an average of 14 strokes and the 2-in-1 needs 8, that is a clear, honest result you can describe to a salon owner: "In our test, hair washed with this combed out in fewer strokes." Keep the notes; they are part of your product file.

Watch the long-term feel too. Ask two or three regular users to use the 2-in-1 for four weeks and report whether hair begins to feel heavy or dull. If it does, lower the polymer level slightly in the next batch, or advise using a plain shampoo once a week. This kind of follow-up is what turns a test product into one that salons reorder.

Cationic polymers work in shampoo because they are used at low levels and are designed for it. Do not try to make a 2-in-1 by pouring a cationic hair conditioner or a quat disinfectant into shampoo. The result is usually cloudy, separated and less effective.

Hot wax and steam

Melted wax at 75 degrees causes serious burns and sticks to skin. Use a double boiler rather than direct flame under the wax pot, keep pot handles turned inwards, wear long sleeves, closed shoes and heat-resistant gloves, and keep children out of the room. If wax or hot liquid touches skin, cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes and seek medical care for anything larger than a small area.
Fixing common conditioner faults
**Thin and watery:** phases not hot enough, or not held long enough to melt fully. Increase heat control or slightly raise cetearyl alcohol in the next batch.
**Grainy or lumpy:** waxes started to set before mixing because one phase was cooler. Heat both to the same temperature.
**Separates after a few days:** too little emulsifier or poor mixing. Mix longer with the stick blender and check weights.
**Heavy, greasy hair:** too much butter or oil for your customers' hair type. Reduce shea or offer it as a separate deep conditioner.

**Bleach and acids** (toilet acids, vinegar, some descalers) release **chlorine gas**, which damages the lungs. **Bleach and ammonia** release **chloramine gases**, which are also toxic. If someone has breathed in fumes from mixed cleaners, the first step is to get them into fresh air at once and seek medical help, especially if they cough, wheeze or feel tightness in the chest. **Cleaning** removes dirt, grease and many germs by washing and rinsing. **Disinfecting** uses a chemical to kill germs that remain on a surface. Dirt and grease shield germs and also use up disinfectant, so the correct order is always: **clean first, rinse, then disinfect**. Hypochlorite (bleach) solutions

Household bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite. The strength is printed on the label and differs between brands, often a few percent. WHO guidance for cleaning environmental surfaces uses a **0.1%** (1,000 ppm) hypochlorite solution for general surfaces, and a stronger **0.5%** solution is used in health settings for spills of blood and body fluids. To make any strength, use the dilution formula: **C1 x V1 = C2 x V2**, where C1 is the bleach strength, V1 the volume of bleach, C2 the strength you want, and V2 the final volume.
Worked example: making 0.1% and 0.5% solutions from 3.5% bleach

For example, Grace manages cleaning at a small private clinic in Ilorin. The bleach label says 3.5% sodium hypochlorite. She needs 10 litres of 0.1% for floors and surfaces, and 2 litres of 0.5% for a spill kit.
0.1% solution: V1 = C2 x V2 / C1 = 0.1 x 10,000 ml / 3.5 = 285.7 ml. She measures about 286 ml of bleach and adds water to make 10 litres in total.
0.5% solution: V1 = 0.5 x 2,000 ml / 3.5 = 285.7 ml. Again about 286 ml of bleach, made up to 2 litres in total.
The same bleach volume gives five times the strength in one fifth of the water, which is a quick check on her arithmetic.
She labels both buckets with the strength, the date and the time, and makes fresh solution every day.
Grace has two correctly diluted solutions, clearly labelled. Because diluted bleach loses strength, she discards leftovers at the end of the day and never tops up an old bucket.
Bleach safety

Dilute with cool water in a ventilated space, wearing gloves and eye protection. Never mix bleach with acids, ammonia or other cleaners. Keep diluted bleach in labelled containers out of sunlight and away from children. Bleach is corrosive to metals and fades fabrics, so rinse metal surfaces after the contact time.
Quaternary ammonium (quat) disinfectants

**Benzalkonium chloride (BKC)** is a common quat, sold as concentrates such as 50% or 80%. Quats are odourless, less corrosive than bleach and widely used in hospitality and salons. Their weaknesses are important: they are **inactivated by soap and anionic detergent residue**, and their effect depends on using the right strength for the right contact time. The use level must come from the registered product's label or the supplier's documented guidance, not from guesswork.
Worked example: diluting a 50% BKC concentrate

For example, suppose a supplier's data sheet says to use the concentrate at 0.2% active for a hard-surface application. (This number is only for practising the arithmetic; always follow the label of the actual product.) Musa needs 10 litres.
Active needed: 10,000 g x 0.2 / 100 = 20 g of BKC (treating 1 litre of dilute solution as about 1 kg).
Concentrate needed: 20 g / 0.50 = 40 g of 50% concentrate.
He weighs 40 g of concentrate into about 9 litres of water, stirs, then tops up to 10 litres.
He labels the bucket with the product, strength, date and the contact time stated on the label.
Musa's solution matches the stated use level exactly, and the label tells staff how long to leave surfaces wet.

Until your product is registered with supported claims, you may sell cleaning products honestly as cleaners, and teach customers to use registered disinfectants correctly. Safety rules you cannot skip

**Never use methanol.** It is poisonous through the skin and if swallowed, and the US FDA has warned about hand sanitisers found to contain methanol. Buy ethanol or isopropyl alcohol from a supplier who gives a certificate of analysis.

**Fire.** Alcohol vapour catches fire easily. Mix in a ventilated room with no flames, no cooking gas, no smoking and no generator nearby. Keep containers closed and store away from heat and sunlight.
**Measure strength.** Use an alcoholmeter (a hydrometer for alcohol) to confirm the incoming alcohol and the final product strength.
**Children.** Swallowing hand rub can poison a child. Use child-resistant or hard-to-open closures for larger bottles and label clearly.

Train their cleaners on doses and the never-mix rules at the first delivery; correct use makes your product perform better and uses less, which builds trust. Three tools of thought
What you will understand
Which surfactant does which job
How pH changes safety and performance
How to keep a water-based product germ-free
Every product in this course, from hand wash to fabric softener, is built on surfactants. You will learn which one does which job.
You will learn how pH changes how safe a product is and how well it works.
And how to keep a product that is mostly water free of germs for its whole shelf life.
How it cleans
Four surfactant families
Anionic: SLES, SLS, LAS. Main cleaners
Amphoteric: CAPB. Milder, more foam
Nonionic: grease cutting, mildness
Cationic: disinfecting, conditioning
A surfactant has a head that loves water and a tail that loves oil. The tails gather into tiny balls called micelles, grab the grease, and rinse water carries it away.
Surfactants are grouped by the electric charge on the head.
Anionic surfactants have a negative charge. SLES, SLS and neutralised sulphonic acid are your main cleaners and foamers.
Amphoteric, like CAPB, makes anionics milder and boosts foam.
Nonionic surfactants have no charge. They cut grease in surface cleaners.
Cationic surfactants are positive. They disinfect, condition hair and soften fabric.
Here is the key rule. Do not mix anionic cleaners with cationic disinfectants or softeners in one product. They attract each other and form a sticky solid that does neither job.
Worked example
Bisi calculates active matter
SLES: 15% x 0.70 = 10.5% active
CAPB: 6% x 0.30 = 1.8% active
Total active matter: 12.3%
New SLES at 60%: use 17.5% of paste
Surfactants are rarely sold pure. SLES paste is commonly about 70% active, and CAPB around 30%. Always read the figure on your supplier's data sheet.
For example, Bisi in Ibadan uses 15% SLES at 70% active. 15% times 0.70 gives 10.5% real surfactant.
She uses 6% CAPB at 30% active. That adds 1.8%.
Her total active matter is 12.3%. She writes it on her formula sheet.
When her new supplier's SLES is only 60% active, she divides 10.5 by 0.60. She needs 17.5% of the new paste, so the product stays the same strength.
pH
Adjust a sample first, then the batch
Weigh a 200 g sample: 1% of 20 kg
Add citric solution in drops, re-test
0.9 g brought it to pH 6.0
0.9 g x 100 = 90 g for the batch
Add about 80% first, then the rest slowly
Always add acid or caustic slowly to water, never water to it.
pH runs from 0 to 14, and 7 is neutral. Each step is a tenfold change, so adjust in small portions. Hand wash and shampoo usually sit around 5 to 7.
Calibrate a pen meter with buffer solutions before use, or it gives confident wrong numbers.
For example, Amaka's 20 kg shampoo reads pH 7.4. She wants about 6. She weighs 200 g into a cup. That is 1% of the batch.
She adds a 20% citric acid solution, stirs and tests, a little at a time.
0.9 g brings the sample to pH 6.0.
She multiplies by 100. The batch needs 90 g.
She adds about 80% first, tests, then adds the rest slowly, so she never overshoots.
Wear gloves and goggles when making adjuster solutions, and add the acid to water, because heat and splashing can result. Label every bottle and keep it from children.
Keep germs out
Liquid soap is mostly water, and water feeds bacteria and mould. A spoiled bottle may smell sour, grow black spots or swell.
Use treated water, or boil it and cool it covered. Wash equipment, then rinse with 70% alcohol. Work with clean hands and covered hair, and use new or sanitised bottles.

Supplier range: pH 3 to 12, 0.5% to 1.0%
Her hand wash is pH 6.2: inside range
Weigh on a digital scale, add when cool

Clean production plus the right preservative

Never pour a conditioner or quat disinfectant into shampoo.
A 2-in-1 shampoo uses a small amount of a cationic polymer. When you rinse, it comes out as a thin film on the hair, so hair tangles less.
For example, Kemi in Abeokuta makes a 2-in-1 for a barbing salon. Her guar supplier recommends 0.2% to 0.5%. She starts at 0.3%.
For 10 kg, that is 30 grams.
These powders form lumps the moment they touch water. So she stirs the guar into the glycerin first, making a smooth slurry.
She pours the slurry into stirring water with a little citric acid.
After 30 minutes it is smooth, with no lumps. Then she continues the normal shampoo method. A wet-combing test, counting comb strokes, proves the difference.
Do not make a 2-in-1 by pouring a cationic conditioner or a quat disinfectant into shampoo. It turns cloudy and separates.
Cream conditioner
The hot-process method
Heat water phase and wax phase to 75 C
Hold 10 to 15 minutes until wax melts
Pour wax phase into water phase, blend
Below 40 C: preservative and fragrance
A rinse-out conditioner is a cream of melted wax and oil held in water. A cationic emulsifier sticks to hair, and a fatty alcohol builds the creamy body.
Weigh the empty pot first. Heat both phases in double boilers to about 75 degrees, checking with a thermometer.
Hold them for 10 to 15 minutes, so all the wax melts.
Pour the wax phase into the water phase while blending. Both must be hot, or the cream turns grainy.
Keep stirring as it cools. It thickens between about 50 and 40 degrees.
Below 40 degrees, add preservative and fragrance, because heat can damage them.
Water lost to heat
Ngozi corrects her batch weight
After cooling, scale reads 6,640 g
Water lost: 160 g
Stir in 160 g of boiled, cooled water
While heating, some water evaporates. For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt makes 5 kg. Her empty pot weighs 1,800 grams, so pot and product should weigh 6,800 grams.
After cooling, the scale reads 6,640 grams.
So 160 grams of water was lost.
She stirs in 160 grams of boiled, cooled water. Without this, every ingredient would be about 3% too concentrated.
Safety
Hot wax, eyes and honest labels
Use a double boiler, long sleeves, heat-resistant gloves. Cool a burn under running water 20 minutes.
Label: 'Avoid contact with eyes. If contact occurs, rinse well with clean water.'
No 'tear-free', 'anti-dandruff' or 'hair growth' without testing and NAFDAC approval.
Melted wax at 75 degrees causes serious burns and sticks to skin. Use a double boiler, not a direct flame, and keep children out.
If wax touches skin, cool it under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Seek medical care for anything larger than a small area.
Most shampoos sting the eyes, so put the eye warning on your label.
And do not write 'tear-free', 'anti-dandruff' or 'hair growth' unless you have the testing and NAFDAC approval for that exact claim.
Remember
Key points from Module 3
Textured hair needs a mild, slightly acidic shampoo
Raise CAPB and add humectants for mildness
Disperse polymer powders as a glycerin slurry
Heat both phases to 75 C; add C below 40 C
Weigh the pot to replace evaporated water
So remember. Keep shampoo mild and slightly acidic. Disperse polymer powders carefully. Control your temperatures, and correct for water lost to heat.

Making a rinse-cycle softener
Warm water to the supplier's temperature
Soften or melt the esterquat
Pour it in slowly, stirring steadily
Below 40 C: fragrance, preservative
Softener goes in the final rinse only, never with detergent.
A softener uses a cationic surfactant called an esterquat. Cotton carries a slight negative charge in water, so the positive softener clings to the fibre and makes it feel soft.
Heat the water to the temperature on your supplier's data sheet.
Warm the esterquat until soft or melted.
Pour it slowly into the warm water while stirring. It turns milky white.
Keep stirring as it cools, then add fragrance and preservative below about 40 degrees. If it is too thick, a little calcium chloride solution thins it.
Softener and detergent combine into a sticky solid, so both stop working. Tell customers: wash and rinse with detergent first, then add softener to the final rinse water only.

Toilet scale only dissolves in acid. A citric acid descaler is slower, but far safer to make, pack and use. It is thickened so it clings under the rim, and packed with a child-resistant cap.

Print and repeat
Many customers believe two cleaners together will be stronger. Bleach and acids release chlorine gas, which damages the lungs. Bleach and ammonia release toxic chloramine gases.
The safe rule: use one product, rinse or flush, then use the next, with the window open.
If someone breathes in fumes from mixed cleaners, get them into fresh air at once and seek medical help. Do not go back into the closed bathroom.

Cleaning removes dirt. Disinfecting kills the germs that remain. Dirt shields germs, so always clean first, rinse, then disinfect, and keep the surface wet for the contact time.
To make any strength, use this formula. Bleach strength times bleach volume equals the strength you want times the final volume.

WHO hand rub
Formulation 1 for 10 litres
Hydrogen peroxide 3%: 417 ml
Glycerol 98%: 145 ml
Water to 10,000 ml: final 80% ethanol
Hold 72 hours before use
WHO publishes a guide so health facilities can make hand rub locally. Following it is the safest starting point, because the formula has a recognised basis.
Formulation 1 uses 8,333 ml of 96% ethanol.
417 ml of 3% hydrogen peroxide helps kill spores in the ingredients or bottles.
145 ml of glycerol protects skin. Then top up with clean water to 10 litres. The result is 80% ethanol.

Rules you cannot skip
Hand rub safety
It is poisonous through the skin and if swallowed. Buy alcohol with a certificate of analysis.
No flames, cooking gas, smoking or generator nearby. Keep containers closed.
Swallowing hand rub can poison a child. Use hard-to-open closures and clear labels.
Never use methanol. It is poisonous through the skin and if swallowed.
Alcohol vapour catches fire easily. Mix in a ventilated room, away from any flame or generator.
And keep it away from children. Remember, hand rub does not replace washing visibly dirty hands with soap and water.
